description.narrative:
Sida har stött UN Transitions Project sedan dess upprättande i 2014 som enda givare. Projektet är ett gemensamt samarbete mellan UNDP, DPO (ansvar för de fredsbevarande trupperna), DPPA (politiska och fredsbyggande avdelningen) samt numera DCO (avdelningen för utvecklingskoordinering, dit FNs Resident Coordinators rapporterar). Det gemensamma projektet lyftes fram av Generalsekreteraren förra året i hans rapport Sustaining Peace (juni 2019) som ett av tre mycket viktiga initiativ för att få ihop FN-systemet gällande fredsbyggande.
Projektperioden gäller en tredje fas av projektet, mellan mitten av 2020 och mitten av 2023. Storbritannien kommer troligtvis att bli delfinansiär tillsammans med Sida, och eventuellt även 1-2 andra givarländer.
Projektet bidrar till fyra huvudmål gällande FN-reformerna; 1. prioritera förebyggande, 2. stärka fältfokus, 3. leverera på Agenda 2030 och 4. bryta ner silos.
Projektets huvudmål är dock att säkerställa att FNs transitioner (övergång) går från en stor fredsbevarande eller politisk mission till att FN organisationer och nationella aktörer på plats bidrar till ett långsiktigt utvecklingsstöd som blir effektivt planerat och styrt. Vilket resulterar i att FN kan leverera resultatorienterat stöd till värdregeringarna samtidigt som transitionen förankras nationellt och engagerar andra aktörer såsom regionala organisationer, civilsamhället och internationella finansiella institutioner.
Projektet har och stödjer nu transitionsprocesser i Elfenbenskusten, Sierra Leone, Haiti, Liberia, Burundi, Sudan, Guinea Bissau, DRC och Mali.
Projektet drivs av ett litet gemensamt sekretariat i New York, samt med sekonderad personal från de inblandade institutionerna. Projektet finansierar också transitionsspecialister på landnivå i fyra länder under kommande fas. Samt har en styrelse bestående av Direktörer från de fyra inblandade institutionerna samt en rådgivande kommitté med bredare medlemskap inom FN-familjen.
Bedömningspromemorian skrivs på engelska med anledning av att den kommer delas med engelskspråkig personal i en större givargrupp samt i fält.

Sida has supported the UN Transitions Project since 2014 as the only donor. The project, which is a joint collaboration between UNDP, DPO (UN Dept for Peace Operations), and DPPA (UN Dept for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs) was highlighted last year (June 2019) by the UN Secretary-General in his interim report on Sustaining Peace, as one of the three key initiatives/processes bringing the UN system together regarding peacebuilding.
This Project period concerns the third phase of the Project, between mid-2020 to mid 2023. United Kingdom/DfiD will likely join Sida as a donor partner for this phase, and probably 1-2 other donor partners.
The Project contributes to four key objectives of the UN reforms: (1) prioritize prevention; (2) strengthen field focus; (3) deliver on the 2030 Agenda; (4) and breaking down the silos. The UN DCO (Development Coordination Office), to which all UN Resident Coordinators report, is now included as the fourth institution in the cooperation.
The project's main task though, is to ensure that UN Transitions from a large UN mission and or political mission to a smaller set up focusing mainly on development, peacebuilding and humanitarian (but not on peacekeeping and less on politicial affairs) are effectively planned and managed, and result in the UN being better positioned to provide efficient and effective support to host countries. The project has and is supporting transitions processes in Ivory Coast, Sierra Leone, Haiti, Liberia, Burundi, Sudan, Guinea Bissau, DRC, and Mali.
The Project is run by a small secretariat in New York, both with project staff and with seconded staff from the involved UN institutions. It is also financing transition specialists in the respective locations and has a Project steering committe with Directors from the cooperating UN institutions, as well as an Advisory Board with broader membership.

The third phase of the UN Transitions Project is designed to contribute to the following objective: Host nations are better equipped to consolidate peacebuilding gains, supported by a nimbler UN that adjusts its strategy and footprint in line with changing circumstances, national peace and development priorities, and in cooperation with key national, regional and international partners. Outcome 1: The UN in transition settings adapts its strategy and footprint in a more pro-active, integrated, and forward-looking manner to support host nations achieve sustainable peace and development Outcome 2: UN Transitions are increasingly prioritized and institutionalized within the UN system and among Member States in a manner reflecting a more effective approach to transition processes The theory of change is; When the UN during and after mission withdrawal reconfigures its full range of peace and development capacities to provide more coherent and effective support, aligned to national priorities and needs, and in a manner that is nationally-led and owned, then host nations in transition settings are better equipped to address root causes of conflict, consolidate peacebuilding gains and take a lead in achieving sustainable peace and development. There are also more detailed theories of change under each outcome in the project application. Below is an overview of the objectives, outcomes and outputs and output indicators, with the overall theory of change to the right.

title.narrative: Agreement Sida UNDP for UN Transition Project 2020-2023
Beslut om insats UN Transition Joint Project 2020-2023

description.narrative:
Results at the global policy level
In recent years, UN Transitions have been working in increasingly challenging environments characterized by complex conflict dynamics, security challenges, strained political relationships and fragile peace processes. Changes in contexts where UN Missions are deployed, for instance, the ongoing withdrawal of MONUSCO in DRC and the host government of Sudan and Mali suddenly requesting the exit of UNITAMS and MINUSMA, have presented challenges to the Transitions project in terms of managing transitions responsibly and sustainably.
These changing dynamics have required the development of new guidance, policies and mechanisms to ensure effective and sustainable support for transitions. It also resulted in an acknowledgement of the importance of proactive transition planning within the UN, leading to an increasing number of requests by the Security Council to begin early transition planning and provide integrated support in various contexts to ensure gradual and sustainable transitions processes. As a response to these requests, The UN Transitions Project has reportedly been providing an increased support to field leadership in a wide range of settings from early transition planning (South Sudan, CAR and Somalia), to ongoing and accelerated transitions (DRC, Mali and Sudan). The Project further worked towards the integration of transition support of UN within the UN system through reviewing the Integrated Assessment and Planning Policy and organizing country-based workshops and trainings of key UN staff. As a result of these efforts, UN staff has an enhanced transition capacity and transitions planning are now a core part of UN processes.
Country-level results
The UN Transitions joint project have engaged in active as well as post-mission transition settings, including the DRC, Mali and Sudan. In DRC, for example, the Transition Specialists have been a crucial actor in negotiations with the Government and in facilitating coordination between MONUSCO, UNCT and provincial governments for transition planning. The Project have further enhanced UNs internal capacity to lead internal and external coordination groups, developing transition plans and strategies, organizing workshops and briefings, and providing advice to MONUSCO and UNCT technical teams. A few achievements include the establishment of Integrated Transition Teams (PITTs) and the organizing of a series of workshops to support the Government in taking over tasks from MONUSCO, addressing peace gains and remaining gaps. Similarly, following the termination of MINUSMAs mandate in 2023, the Project, among other forms of support, delivered surge capacity to Bamako and supported the process of transferring tasks from MINUSMA to AFPs and ensuring coordination between HQ and local entities.
The Project have further provided crucial support in early transitions settings, including South Sudan, Central African Republic (CAR) and Somalia. Following MINUSCAs new mandate in 2023 and the request from the Security Council to provide a strategic plan and recommendations of a potential withdrawal in CAR, the UN Transition Project assisted in the early transition process. The Project facilitated a session on early transition planning during the UNCT retreat in Bangui in October 2023. The session marked the first time UNCT leadership convened to discuss this topic, focusing on joint analysis, joint planning, joint resource mobilization and financing as well as UN coordination. According to UN Transition reporting, as a result, collaboration and coordination between MINUSCA and UNCT was enhanced, with a emphasis on HDP collaboration and UN integration.
In South Sudan, the Security Council requested an integrated UN transition strategy to build durable peace and self-reliance in October 2023. In response to this request, the Project facilitated a leadership retreat and technical planning workshop in collaboration with the DPO-DPPA South Sudan Integrated Operational Team. Key results include the establishment of joint principals for early transition planning, agreeing on five transition pillars, and a Transition Roadmap with concrete steps and milestones. To implement this, the Project deployed a Risk and Conflict Analysis Advisor to the Office of the DSRSG/RC/HC.
Policy and Guidance
During 2023, the UN Transitions Project advanced its policy and guidance development and implementation efforts, focusing on energy transitions, gender responsiveness, organizational learning and practice building. For example, the Project carried out some efforts to improve the energy access in fragile and conflict-affected states. These efforts have led to increased collaboration among missions, host governments, and other stakeholders on renewable energy initiatives and a prioritization of renewable energy in transition planning. The Project further collaborated with gender advisors from various UN departments and agencies to develop a Practitioners Note, aiming to ensure that UN transitions are planned with a gender-responsive approach, providing missions, UNCT and HQ staff with practical advice.
To enhance capacity-building, collaboration and equip UN staff with the skills needed for effective transition planning, the UN Transition Project hosted transition planning trainings, briefings, webinars and workshops for both field and HQ staff from various contexts, for example CAR, South Sudan and Somalia. Key achievements from these efforts include enhanced technical expertise among key staff and a greater collaboration between field and HQ staff, as well as a deeper understanding for crucial aspects such as the Transition Roadmap. The Project also prioritized partnerships with Member States, the EU, the World Bank and other actors, to ensure successful transitions from UN missions to Country Teams. One notable example is the joint UN-EU workshop held in the DRC, which emphasized cooperation in areas like DDR and Protection of civilians.
